Why your personal return can differ from the investment’s return

Separate account growth from contributions, link an invented fund return path, and calculate a one-year money-weighted return using the amount and timing of new money.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore one invented return path and the date of one contribution

Interactive planning lab

Time-weighted return for the invented year0.00%
Money-weighted annual return for the entered cash timing16.89%
Investment gain or loss, excluding the contribution$2,500

One invented year of twelve equal month fractions. Each six-month return is spread evenly through its six months; the contribution arrives after the selected month’s return. There are no withdrawals, distributions, fees or taxes. Time-weighted return links the fund-growth factors independently of external contributions. Money-weighted return solves the unique annual cash-flow equation using the opening investment, one nonnegative contribution and positive ending value. No actual statement convention, daily XIRR, manager evaluation or future timing recommendation is provided.

The central idea

Time-weighted return follows the investment path independently of external cash flows. Money-weighted return also reflects how much money was exposed to each part of that path.

01

Start by separating account balance from investment performance

A larger year-end investment account can reflect gains, new contributions or both. The opening and closing balances alone cannot tell you which. Before interpreting a return percentage, reconcile the external cash that entered or left the account during the measurement period.

This invented example starts with CAD 10,000. The investment loses 20% over the first six months and gains 25% over the next six. Another CAD 10,000 arrives immediately after month six’s return, and there are no withdrawals, distributions, taxes or fees.

The account finishes at CAD 22,500. Of the CAD 12,500 increase from its opening balance, CAD 10,000 is new money. The remaining CAD 2,500 is investment gain. The waterfall makes those components explicit. Dividing the entire balance increase by the opening investment would label an external deposit as profit and produce a misleading percentage.

02

Link the investment’s return factors

The first CAD 10,000 falls to CAD 8,000 by the end of the first half. A 25% gain then brings that original exposure back to CAD 10,000. The linked annual return is (1 − 0.20) × (1 + 0.25) − 1 = 0%.

Adding negative 20% and positive 25% would instead give positive 5%, which is not the compounded result. The second percentage applies to the smaller value after the first loss. A percentage recovery must be read against its own starting base.

The normalized chart applies the same factors to an unchanged CAD 1,000 investment. It reaches CAD 800 at month six and CAD 1,000 at year-end. No external money enters that line, so its ending-to-opening ratio isolates the linked investment return.

In the interactive example, each six-month total return is spread evenly across its six months using equivalent compound factors. The smooth-looking path is a modeling choice, not observed daily prices or evidence that markets move evenly.

03

See which money experienced each part of the year

The new CAD 10,000 enters after the first-half loss. It therefore does not experience that loss in the selected scenario. It is exposed to the second-half 25% gain and becomes CAD 12,500. Combined with CAD 10,000 from the recovered original investment, this explains the CAD 22,500 ending account.

The account chart shows a vertical step from CAD 8,000 to CAD 18,000 at month six. Two observations at that date represent values immediately before and after the contribution. The jump is external cash arriving; it is not a sudden market return.

Consequently, the investment’s zero linked return and the account’s positive dollar gain can both be correct. More money was present during the favorable half of this particular invented year. The result does not mean an account holder or manager generated an additional 25% return on all the money for the entire year.

04

Solve a rate that respects the contribution date

A money-weighted return fits a compound rate to the dated account cash flows and ending value. Here the annual rate r satisfies 10,000 × (1 + r) + 10,000 × (1 + r)0.5 = 22,500. The first amount is present for one year and the second for half a year.

The solution is approximately 16.89%. It is an annual money-weighted rate for this one-year horizon, rather than a claim that every dollar earned 16.89% during its actual holding time. Using the common annual factor over each amount’s exposure period reconciles the final value.

Dividing the CAD 2,500 gain by CAD 20,000 of total deposits gives 12.5%. That simple ratio ignores how long the second deposit was invested. It is therefore a different calculation from the money-weighted rate and from the linked time-weighted return.

The calculator uses twelve equal month fractions and solves one unique positive growth factor. It is not a daily XIRR tool, and real statement date conventions, charges and additional cash flows can produce different reported figures.

05

Compare alternative dates without treating hindsight as a plan

The final chart moves the same contribution across twelve possible month-end dates while retaining the selected return path. Every point is a separate complete-year scenario. It is not the year-to-date return earned by the corresponding month.

The time-weighted line stays fixed because the underlying investment path is unchanged. The money-weighted line can move because the new money experiences different portions of that path. If the contribution is zero, the two methods coincide in this simplified account.

A contribution after month twelve also leaves the two rates equal: it arrives at the terminal date and has no time to earn a return inside the measured year. Its cash still raises the final balance, but the money-weighted equation assigns it zero exposure time.

The displayed path is already known because it was invented for teaching. A favorable date in this comparison cannot identify the future best date to invest. Planning decisions need to account for available cash, goals, risk and uncertainty rather than selecting a past turning point after seeing the outcome.

06

Read the method and period beside an actual return

Fidelity Canada’s investor education distinguishes time-weighted investment performance from dollar-weighted personal performance, which reflects the amount and timing of account cash flows. Those descriptions explain why two percentages can answer different questions.

Before comparing actual statements or a fund fact sheet, align the period, currency, fee treatment and return method. Confirm which transfers count as external flows and whether an account number includes cash or several investments. A method label does not make mismatched periods or different portfolios directly comparable.

Use the cash reconciliation to understand the dollars and the return methodology to understand the percentage. Neither replaces the other. This article supplies transparent arithmetic for one contribution, while an actual multi-transaction account needs its complete dated flow history and the provider’s stated conventions.
